I recommend keeping the long run around 10 km easy this week and not expanding the tempo work. Your longest recorded run is 10.206 km: 13 km would add 27.4%. You have usually run twice weekly, totaling 13–19 km, while three moderate-to-hard climbing sessions also require recovery. The proposed 100 minutes is a scheduling estimate, compared with about 67 minutes moving and 75 minutes elapsed on that recorded run; it is not a measured increase in physiological load. Your fresh energy, normal sleep and lack of pain support training, but do not establish tolerance of the extension.

13 km within a 23 km week is 56.5%, within the structural ceiling, but that ratio does not establish readiness. We have only five weekly totals and incomplete activity coverage, so 10.206 km is the longest recorded run, not a proven maximum. Resolve the missing recording and review the additional recent week before finalizing the proposal. Keep the tempo at 10 km only if that is an established, comfortable dose; if fatigue or difficult finishing develops, shorten the run and reduce quality work. Adding a third run or filler distance is not the solution.

I support a 17 km easy long run in the next-week proposal. The relevant completed comparator is your comfortable 15 km, still inside the preceding 30 days; the 9.5 km recovery run does not reset it. That makes 17 km a 13.3% extension, not a jump from 9.5 km. Your normal recovery, sleep and energy, with no pain, support this coaching judgment; an increase above 10% is not automatically unacceptable.

Your 15 km took about 102 minutes moving and 108 minutes elapsed. Allow for a longer outing at easy effort; we do not yet have a reliable duration estimate for 17 km. In a 31 km week, the long run is 54.8%, leaving 14 km across the other two runs. Keep that supporting work familiar and avoid combining the extension with new intensity or an unsupported frequency increase. The broader consistency history is not supplied here, so that remains uncertain. If the outing feels unusually taxing, shorten toward 15 km, and stop for pain. The exact workouts still need review and your approval; 17 km is not a completed achievement.

No—I recommend rebuilding near your recent completed distance, around 10 km easy, rather than going straight to 17 km. Neither the planned 13 km nor the planned 15 km happened. Your longest completed comparator remains 10.206 km, making 17 km about a 66.6% extension. Being pain-free is encouraging, but does not replace those missing endurance sessions.

The approved 17 km target depended on comfortable prior completion and recovery, so its prerequisite is unmet. We should revise the remaining targets within this same goal and training cycle, then review and approve the replacement week. Do not cram the missed distance into other runs. Progress again from actual comfortable completion and normal recovery; if fatigue or pain appears, shorten or pause and reassess.

Do not do the 15 km long run next week. You completed 9 km and stopped because of knee pain, which persists today; that is a reason to reassess, regardless of normal sleep or the approved strategic target.

Pause running while the knee remains painful and arrange an assessment with a qualified clinician or physiotherapist, particularly if pain is worsening or affects walking. We should defer the upcoming long-run progression and revise the week after understanding the symptoms and recovery. I would not prescribe a replacement distance or approve the exact week yet. The planned 13 km was not completed, and neither it nor the planned 15 km proves current capacity.

No. The first athlete is considering 12 km after 11 km, a 9.1% extension, within a 20 km week after 19 km. The second is considering 36 km after 28 km, a 28.6% extension, while weekly distance rises from 52 to 60 km. Those are very different absolute sessions and combined changes.

With two running days, the first athlete has 8 km of supporting running; with three, the second has 24 km. Both long runs occupy 60%, but the ratio only describes structure. I would consider 12 km provisionally reasonable if previous finishing and recovery were comfortable, while holding the second athlete near the demonstrated 28 km until duration, experience and recovery evidence justify an extension. Neither being below 10% nor reporting no recent pain guarantees tolerance. Review time on feet, terrain, quality work and individual recovery before finalizing either week; shorten if difficult finishing or persistent fatigue emerges. Do not add filler distance to improve the percentage.

I recommend keeping the recovery week at 18 km, easy only, with the 9.5 km long run. Your longest recorded completion is 10.206 km; the planned 13 km is not yet synchronized evidence. Extending the recovery run would add exposure before we have seen how you finish and recover from the preceding progression.

No climbing applies only to Barcelona, 19–25 October; your normal three-session routine stays intact. That removes one expected demand for this week, but travel, walking, heat, hills and disrupted sleep can still add fatigue. Before selecting workout days, review the local forecast and those travel demands. If they are taxing, shorten the runs rather than extending them.

HR under 150 may support comfortable aerobic effort in your personal context, but it does not prove tolerance of extra distance. An easy pace a minute per kilometre slower than goal pace neither disproves the half-marathon goal nor predicts it. Normal sleep and no pain are encouraging; they do not remove the purpose of a recovery week.

I recommend a recovery-focused week with less total distance, a shorter easy long run and reduced quality work. Your completed 13 km took 100 minutes elapsed, ended with two difficult kilometres, and required three days of recovery; energy is still below normal. That argues against progressing to 15 km or shifting the removed distance into the other runs.

Prepare a same-goal amendment to lower the approved 28 km target and soften the upcoming progression, then review replacement workouts for your approval. Keep up to three running days without lengthening the supporting runs; tentatively bring the long run back toward 10 km, subject to restored energy and comfortable easy running. Until recovery is normal, defer the tempo and the longer session. If energy remains low, shorten further or rest and reassess. This is a revision recommendation, not an approval-ready week, and it does not change completed training.

Two hours is a plausible goal, but I cannot honestly call it likely from the current evidence. Your owned 5 km assessment of 25:15 and approved VDOT 38 give a half-marathon performance equivalence around 1:56:13. That supports the speed side of the goal; it is not an endurance forecast.

Most weeks have only two runs and 13–19 km, with a longest recorded run of 10.206 km. The planned 13, 15 and 17 km sessions are future targets, not demonstrated preparation. Incomplete activity coverage also means the recorded longest run may not be your true longest. Fresh energy, normal sleep and no pain help, but do not settle half-marathon endurance.

Your easy pace being a minute per kilometre slower than goal pace is not evidence against the goal, and HR under 150 does not prove race readiness. My recommendation is to retain two hours as provisional and reassess from actual longer-run completion, finishing comfort and subsequent recovery before the race on 14 November. If those runs are missed or recovery becomes difficult, use a more conservative race effort instead of forcing the time target. I would not assign a success percentage or derive training paces from VDOT.
